Product confirms the two promotions must not stack. A teammate proposes adding `total = max(total, 0)` at the end of `checkout()`. What is the best response?

options.text: Reject it; first write a test reproducing the double discount, fix the stacking rule in `apply_discount`, then search for other places that apply promotions the same way
options.explanation: Correct. Establish the intended stacking rule, reproduce the violation in a test, then fix and validate the relevant logic. The test demonstrates the case; investigation connects it to the cause. Check other consumers and paths as well.

options.text: Accept it; the customer never sees a negative total, so the bug is fixed
options.explanation: This hides the symptom. Discounts that should not stack still stack, and other code that reads the discount (refunds, reports, revenue) still sees the wrong value.

options.text: Reject it and remove all promotions until a full rewrite is ready
options.explanation: Disproportionate. The cause is understood and can be fixed precisely.

options.text: Accept it but log a warning; logs are enough to track the issue
options.explanation: Logging a symptom you have already diagnosed defers the real fix and still leaves wrong discount data elsewhere.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask *why* the total went negative: two promotions both applied in full.
2. That is a business-rule bug in `apply_discount`. Fixing it there corrects every consumer of the discount, not just `checkout`.
3. Write the test first: basket £20, two £15 promotions, expect the rule you agree with product (e.g. best single promotion, total £5).
4. Fix, watch it pass, run the suite.
5. Search for other code paths that apply promotions (e.g. the mobile API) and check them too.
6. A `max(…, 0)` guard plus an alert can stay as a safety net, but it is not the fix.

questions.prompt: You have spent two hours on a bug. You have changed several settings, reverted some, and are no longer sure what state the system is in. Which actions follow methodical debugging practice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Return to a known state (clean checkout, default config) and re-establish the reproduction
options.explanation: Correct. You cannot reason from an unknown starting point. Reset, then confirm the bug still reproduces.

options.text: Write down the hypotheses already tested and their results before continuing
options.explanation: Correct. An audit trail stops you re-testing the same idea and often exposes a gap in the reasoning.

options.text: Explain the problem step by step to a colleague or a rubber duck
options.explanation: Correct. Saying your assumptions aloud often reveals the false one; a fresh view is one of Agans' rules.

options.text: Change several more settings at once to save time
options.explanation: Unplanned simultaneous changes created the confusion. One controlled change at a time is a useful way to make effects easier to attribute.

options.text: Check basic assumptions, such as whether the code you are editing is the code that is actually running
options.explanation: Correct. 'Check the plug': stale builds, the wrong config file, or testing against the wrong host are surprisingly common.

questions.workedExample:
Map each to a principle:

- A: make it fail from a known state.
- B: keep an audit trail.
- C: get a fresh view.
- E: check the plug (question your assumptions).
- D: violates 'change one thing at a time'.

After two hours, the most productive next step is usually A plus E: reset and verify the basics.

questions.prompt: A user reports a bug. Which reproduction is most valuable to have before you start changing code?

options.text: A screen recording of the user hitting the bug once
options.explanation: Useful evidence, but you cannot rerun it after a fix to confirm the bug is gone.

options.text: A description from the user of roughly what they were doing
options.explanation: A starting point for investigation, not a reproduction.

options.text: An automated test that fails in seconds on the current code
options.explanation: Correct. It is reliable, fast and repeatable: you can run it after every hypothesis, and once the fix lands it becomes a regression test.

options.text: A production log line showing the error
options.explanation: Logs show *that* it happened, and help form hypotheses, but you cannot rerun a log line to check a fix.

questions.workedExample:
A good reproduction is reliable, fast and automated.

1. Use the report, recording and logs to work out the triggering inputs.
2. Encode those inputs as a test. Confirm it fails for the same reason the user saw.
3. Now every experiment takes seconds, and 'fixed' has an objective meaning: the test passes.
4. Keep the test, to detect recurrence of the covered scenario.

lessons.title: Profiling and performance work
lessons.summary: How to make code faster without guessing - set a target, benchmark honestly, use Amdahl's law, read cProfile output and flame graphs, tell CPU time from waiting, and go after the wins that actually matter.
lessons.body:
A useful rule for performance work is: **measure before you change anything**. Intuition can misidentify where time goes. For example: The loop you were sure was slow takes 2% of the runtime; the real cost is a database call hidden inside a helper.

This lesson covers a disciplined workflow: define the goal, measure, find the bottleneck, change one thing, and measure again.

## When to optimise

Donald Knuth's famous line, from a 1974 paper, is usually quoted only in part:

> We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%.

The point is not "never optimise". It is: do not contort code for speed before you know it matters, and when it does matter, measure which parts matter and work there. The quoted percentages are rhetorical guidance, not measured proportions for every program.

Start with a **concrete target** tied to users or cost:

- **Latency**: "p99 of `/search` under 300 ms" (the 99th percentile, roughly 1% of observations lie above it, depending on ties and the percentile convention).
- **Throughput**: "the nightly import finishes within its 2-hour window".
- **Resources**: "fit in a 512 MB container", "halve the CPU bill".

Without a target you cannot tell when to stop, and performance work has no natural end.

> [!tip] Use percentiles, not averages
> A mean of 80 ms can hide a p99 of 2 seconds. Users making more requests have more opportunities to encounter slow requests, though request types and latency dependence also matter.

## Amdahl's law: where the ceiling is

If part of a program takes fraction *p* of the runtime, and you make that part *s* times faster, the overall speedup for fixed work, assuming the remaining runtime is unchanged, is:

```
speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / s)
```

Suppose a function takes 30% of runtime and you make it 10 times faster:

```
1 / (0.7 + 0.3 / 10)
= 1 / (0.7 + 0.03)
= 1 / 0.73
≈ 1.37x
```

Even making it infinitely fast only gives 1 / 0.7 ≈ 1.43×. The 70% you did not touch caps the gain. The lesson: work on the biggest slice first, and a profiler tells you which slice that is.

## Step 1: benchmark honestly

A **benchmark** measures how long something takes, so you can compare before and after. Easy to do, easy to do badly.

For small snippets, Python's `timeit` runs code many times and handles timer details:

```python
import timeit

setup = "s = set(range(100_000))"
runs = timeit.repeat("-1 in s",
                     setup=setup,
                     number=100_000,
                     repeat=5)
print(min(runs))
```

The `timeit` docs recommend looking at the minimum of the repeats: higher values are usually caused by other processes interfering, not by your code.

Common benchmarking mistakes:

- **Unrealistic data.** An algorithm that is fine with 100 rows can be quadratic at 100,000. Use production-sized inputs.
- **Mismatched warm-up.** Warm up for steady-state measurements; measure cold starts separately if that is the target. The first run can pay for cold caches, lazy imports, connection setup and JIT compilation (in PyPy, the JVM or V8).
- **Noise.** Laptops throttle, browsers steal CPU. Repeat runs and compare distributions, not single numbers.
- **Measuring the wrong thing.** A micro-benchmark of string concatenation tells you nothing if the request spends 90% of its time waiting for Postgres.

## Step 2: profile to find the bottleneck

A **profiler** tells you where time goes. There are two main kinds.

| Kind | How it works | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic | Hooks every call and return | `cProfile` |
| Sampling | Records stacks N times/sec | `py-spy`, `perf` |

**Deterministic** profilers count observed call events in the profiled execution scope, with overhead that can disproportionately affect tiny functions. **Sampling** profilers periodically capture stacks; some interrupt execution while tools such as py-spy read another process externally. Sampling is approximate and often lower overhead, but production use requires suitable permissions and validation of workload impact. `py-spy` can attach to a running Python process by PID without restarting it.

### Reading cProfile

```
python -m cProfile -s cumtime app.py
```

Illustrative output, with some columns trimmed:

```
ncalls  tottime  cumtime  function
     1    0.002    9.810  main
  5000    0.150    9.420  load_order
  5000    9.100    9.100  db.query
200000    0.310    0.310  fmt_price
```

- **ncalls**: how many times it was called.
- **tottime**: time spent in the function itself, *excluding* functions it called.
- **cumtime**: time *including* everything it called.

Read it like this: `main` takes 9.8 s cumulatively but almost none itself. Nearly all of it is under `load_order`, and within that `db.query` has a tottime of 9.1 s from 5,000 calls. Repeated per-order queries suggest an **N+1 query** pattern if an initial query fetched the orders. Investigate batching or joining and measure the resulting database work; the profile alone does not guarantee the saving. `fmt_price` is called 200,000 times but costs only 0.3 s; optimising it cannot remove more than its measured contribution under these assumptions.

### Reading a flame graph

A **flame graph** (Brendan Gregg's visualisation) shows sampled stacks:

```
[       fmt       ][   db.query    ]
[        load_order                ]
[             main                 ]
```

- Each box is a function; the box above it is something it called.
- **Width** is the share of samples that included that function: for a CPU-time graph, wider estimates more CPU time. Other flame graphs can encode off-CPU time or allocation volume.
- The x-axis is *not* time. Boxes are sorted (often alphabetically) so identical stacks merge.
- Look for wide plateaus near the top: in a CPU-sampled graph with complete stack unwinding, these indicate self CPU time rather than just callees.

## CPU time versus waiting

A request can be slow while the CPU is idle. It may be waiting for a database, a network call, a lock or the disk. This is **off-CPU** time, and a CPU-only profiler will not show it, because a sleeping thread is not on the CPU to be sampled.

Compare **wall-clock time** (what the user experiences) with **CPU time** (what the process actually computed). If a request takes 800 ms of wall time and 20 ms of CPU time, optimising Python code cannot help much; look at what it waits for, including time runnable but waiting for CPU scheduling. A low CPU time for one request does not show that the whole machine is idle. Distributed tracing, database slow-query logs and wall-clock profiling modes are the right tools there.

For whole machines, Gregg's **USE method** is a quick checklist: for each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check **Utilisation**, **Saturation** (queued work) and **Errors**.

## Step 3: the wins that matter

Candidate improvements to evaluate against measurements:

1. **Do less work.** Remove repeated computation, unneeded fields, duplicate calls.
2. **Better algorithms and data structures.** O(n²) to O(n log n) beats any micro-optimisation once n is large.
3. **Batch I/O.** One query for 5,000 rows instead of 5,000 queries. Batch API calls, buffer writes.
4. **Cache** results that are expensive and reused, with a plan for invalidation.
5. **Concurrency** for I/O-bound work (asyncio, threads): overlap the waits.
6. **Move hot loops** to optimised code: NumPy vectorisation, a C extension, or a compiled language.
7. **Micro-optimisations** (local variable lookups, avoiding attribute access) last, and only in a proven hot loop.

A very common example of point 2:

```python
def common(a, b):
    # 'x in b' scans the list: O(m)
    return [x for x in a if x in b]

def common_fast(a, b):
    bs = set(b)  # O(m) once
    # 'x in bs' is O(1) on average
    return [x for x in a if x in bs]
```

With 10,000 items in each list, `common` does up to 100 million comparisons; `common_fast` does about 20,000 operations. This is an asymptotic comparison, not a measured timing guarantee. It assumes stable, hashable values and effectively constant-time equality/hashing; the set uses O(m) additional memory. Unhashable values or unusual equality semantics can invalidate this replacement. No universal seconds-to-milliseconds result is included because it cannot be reliably established without a specified workload and benchmark.

### Memory

Memory problems show up as growing RSS, swapping, or the container being OOM-killed. Python's `tracemalloc` takes snapshots of allocations; comparing two snapshots shows which lines allocated the memory that grew:

```python
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
retained = [bytearray(1024)
            for _ in range(100)]
snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
diff = snap2.compare_to(snap1, "lineno")
for stat in diff[:5]:
    print(stat)
```

Typical culprits are unbounded caches, lists that grow for the lifetime of a process, and objects retained by callbacks or other references. Python normally collects unreachable reference cycles; cycles alone do not establish a leak. tracemalloc covers traced Python allocations, not every native allocation or all RSS.

## Step 4: verify and protect

After a change, re-run the **same benchmark**, on the same machine and data. Keep the change only if it moved the target metric meaningfully. Then protect the gain: a performance test in CI with a generous threshold, or production dashboards that alert on regressions. Speed lost a little at a time in later commits is common and hard to notice.

## Pitfalls

- **Optimising without a profile.** The most common mistake, and the most wasted effort.
- **Trusting micro-benchmarks** for macro decisions. Measure the real workload too.
- **Ignoring the tail.** Improving the median while p99 gets worse can make the product feel slower.
- **Sacrificing clarity for tiny gains.** Unreadable code has its own cost. Comment any non-obvious optimisation with the measurement that justified it.
- **Load tests that hide latency.** A load generator that waits for each response before sending the next one sends fewer requests exactly when the system slows down, so it under-reports bad latency. This is **coordinated omission**; for an independently arriving production workload, tools like wrk2 schedule a target arrival rate and measure latency from intended send times. Constant rate alone is insufficient if delayed sends are omitted from latency. A closed-loop model can be appropriate when the real workload is closed-loop.

## Key takeaways
- Set a concrete target (p99 latency, throughput, memory) and measure before changing anything.
- Amdahl's law caps the gain from speeding up one part; profile to find the biggest slice.
- Deterministic profilers count observed calls with overhead; sampling profilers estimate stack prevalence and require production overhead/permission checks.
- In cProfile, tottime is self time and cumtime includes callees; in CPU flame graphs, width estimates CPU time and the x-axis is not chronological.
- Slow but idle usually means waiting on I/O or locks. Algorithms, batching and caching beat micro-optimisation.

## Further reading
- [The Python Profilers — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/profile.html)
- [timeit — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/timeit.html)
- [tracemalloc — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/tracemalloc.html)
- [py-spy — sampling profiler for Python (GitHub)](https://github.com/benfred/py-spy)
- [Flame Graphs — Brendan Gregg](https://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html)
- [The USE Method — Brendan Gregg](https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html)
- [Amdahl's law — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)

questions.prompt: A report job takes 100 seconds. Profiling shows a parsing function accounts for 40 seconds. You make that function 4 times faster. What is the new total runtime?

options.text: 25 seconds
options.explanation: This applies the 4× speedup to the whole job. Only the 40 seconds of parsing gets faster; the other 60 seconds are unchanged.

options.text: 70 seconds
options.explanation: Correct. Parsing drops from 40 s to 10 s; the other 60 s are untouched. 60 + 10 = 70 s, an overall speedup of about 1.43×.

options.text: 90 seconds
options.explanation: This subtracts only 10 seconds. Parsing goes from 40 s to 40 / 4 = 10 s, which saves 30 s.

options.text: 60 seconds
options.explanation: 60 s is the runtime if parsing became instant. A 4× speedup still leaves 10 s of parsing.

questions.workedExample:
1. Split the runtime: 40 s parsing, 60 s everything else.
2. New parsing time: 40 / 4 = 10 s.
3. New total: 60 + 10 = **70 s**.
4. With Amdahl's law: p = 0.4, s = 4:

```
1 / (0.6 + 0.4/4)
= 1 / 0.7
≈ 1.43x  ->  100 / 1.43 = 70 s
```

Even an infinite speedup of parsing would only reach 60 s.

questions.prompt:
Assume constant-time equality comparisons. What is the worst-case time complexity of this function, where `a` and `b` are both lists of length n?

```python
def common(a, b):
    return [x for x in a if x in b]
```

options.text: O(n)
options.explanation: This would be true if `b` were a set. For a list, `x in b` scans elements one by one.

options.text: O(n log n)
options.explanation: No sorting or binary search happens here; the membership test is a linear scan.

options.text: O(n²)
options.explanation: Correct. For each of the n elements of `a`, `x in b` scans up to n elements of `b`: n × n comparisons in the worst case.
The function must at least look at every element of `a`, so it cannot be constant time.

questions.workedExample:
1. The comprehension loops over `a`: n iterations.
2. Each iteration evaluates `x in b`. For a list, that is a linear scan: up to n comparisons.
3. Total: n × n = O(n²). With n = 10,000 that is up to 100 million comparisons.
4. Fix: `bs = set(b)` first (O(n)), then `x in bs` is O(1) on average, giving O(n) overall. The set replacement requires stable hashable values and uses O(n) extra memory; hash collisions can worsen its worst case.

questions.prompt: Your team wants to speed up an API. A developer suggests rewriting the JSON serialisation in Rust because "JSON is always slow". What should happen first?

options.text: Do the rewrite; serialisation is a well-known bottleneck
options.explanation: It might be, but without measurement you could spend weeks speeding up something that takes 2% of each request.

options.text: Set a target (for example p99 latency) and profile real requests to find where the time actually goes
options.explanation: Correct. A target says when you are done, and a profile tells you which part is worth working on. Guesses about bottlenecks are wrong surprisingly often.

options.text: Add more servers instead
options.explanation: More servers can reduce queueing latency when capacity is the bottleneck, but measuring the bottleneck should precede the decision.

options.text: Turn on caching for every endpoint
options.explanation: Caching can help, but applying it everywhere without knowing the bottleneck adds staleness and complexity, possibly for no gain.

questions.workedExample:
1. Define success: e.g. 'p99 of /orders below 250 ms'. Measure the current value.
2. Profile representative requests, including wall-clock time, not just CPU.
3. Suppose serialisation is 3% of time and a database call is 70%. By Amdahl's law, an infinitely fast serialiser saves at most 3%.
4. Work on the biggest slice, re-measure, and stop when the target is met.

questions.prompt:
Here is part of a cProfile report (some columns trimmed):

```
ncalls tottime cumtime function
     1   0.01   12.40  run
  2000   0.20   12.10  handle
  2000  11.50   11.50  http_get
 90000   0.25    0.25  parse_row
```

Which change would most likely give the biggest improvement?

options.text: Optimise `parse_row`, because it is called 90,000 times
options.explanation: Call count is not cost. `parse_row` costs 0.25 s in total, about 2% of the runtime.

options.text: Optimise `run`, because it has the largest cumtime
options.explanation: `run`'s cumtime includes everything it calls. Its own tottime is 0.01 s; there is nothing to optimise inside it.

options.text: Reduce the time spent in `http_get`, for example by batching requests or making them concurrent
options.explanation: Correct. This is the dominant measured cost. Inspect whether it is waiting, computing or retrying before choosing batching or concurrency.

options.text: Optimise `handle`, because it calls `http_get`
options.explanation: `handle` itself only spends 0.2 s. Its large cumtime comes from `http_get`; you change `handle` only insofar as it decides how `http_get` is called.

questions.workedExample: http_get accounts for 11.5/12.4 ≈ 93% of runtime, or 5.75 ms per call. The name and profile do not prove network waiting. If measurements confirm independent equal-duration I/O calls and sufficient downstream capacity, 20-way overlap has an ideal call-time floor of 11.5/20 = 0.575 s, before overhead. Batching and concurrency must preserve ordering, side effects and rate limits.

questions.prompt: In a CPU-sampled flame graph with complete stack unwinding of a web service, what does a very wide box near the **top** of a stack indicate?

options.text: A function that ran for a long time early in the recording, since the x-axis is time
options.explanation: The x-axis in a standard flame graph is not time; stacks are sorted (often alphabetically) and merged. Use a 'flame chart' if you need a timeline.

options.text: A function that appeared in many samples and was itself running on the CPU, rather than just calling other functions
options.explanation: Correct. Width is the proportion of samples containing the function. Near the top means few or no callees above it, so the time is spent in the function itself: a prime optimisation target.

options.text: A function with a very deep call stack
options.explanation: Stack depth is shown by height (how many boxes are stacked), not width.

options.text: A function that was called many times
options.explanation: Flame graphs from sampling profilers show time (samples), not call counts. One long call and many short ones can look the same width.

questions.workedExample:
1. Y-axis: stack depth. Each box's parent is directly below it.
2. Width: share of samples in which the function appeared on the stack.
3. A wide box with nothing (or little) above it is on-CPU itself in many samples.
4. A wide box with wide children is just a caller; follow the width upwards.
5. The x-axis order has no meaning; boxes are sorted so identical stacks merge.

questions.prompt: An endpoint takes 900 ms of wall-clock time, but the process uses only about 30 ms of CPU time per request. A CPU sampling profiler shows nothing interesting. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The profiler is broken; CPU profiles always explain latency
options.explanation: CPU profilers only see threads that are running on a CPU. Time spent blocked does not appear.

options.text: The Python interpreter is too slow; rewrite in a compiled language
options.explanation: Only 30 ms is spent computing. A compiled language might shave some of that, but the 870 ms of waiting would remain.

options.text: The machine needs more CPU cores
options.explanation: Low CPU time for one request does not prove the machine is idle. More cores may help scheduler queueing, but first identify whether the delay is scheduling, I/O or locks.

options.text: The request spends most of its time off-CPU, potentially waiting on I/O, locks or CPU scheduling
options.explanation: Correct. 870 ms of the 900 ms is waiting. Look at tracing, slow-query logs, connection pool waits and lock contention, or use a wall-clock or off-CPU profiler.

questions.workedExample:
1. Wall time 900 ms, CPU time 30 ms: about 97% of the time the request is not computing.
2. A sampling CPU profiler records stacks of on-CPU threads, so blocked time is invisible to it.
3. Candidates: slow queries, N+1 queries, remote API calls, exhausted connection pools, lock waits, or runnable time waiting for a CPU.
4. Tools: distributed traces with spans per call, database slow-query logs, or off-CPU / wall-clock profiling (py-spy's `--idle` option includes idle stacks).

questions.prompt: You compare two implementations with a steady-state benchmark. Which practices make the result more trustworthy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run each version many times and compare the distributions (or the minimum, for a micro-benchmark)
options.explanation: Correct. One run is dominated by noise; repeats show the real difference.

options.text: Use input sizes similar to production
options.explanation: Correct. Complexity differences only show at scale; an O(n²) algorithm can look fine on 100 items.

options.text: Include a warm-up phase before measuring
options.explanation: Correct. Cold caches, lazy imports, connection setup and JIT compilation distort the first iterations.

options.text: Run the old version on your laptop and the new one on a CI server
options.explanation: Different hardware and load make the comparison meaningless. Benchmarks must run on the same machine under the same conditions.

options.text: Run the benchmark once and report the number to three decimal places
options.explanation: Precision is not accuracy. A single run can vary by tens of percent; three decimal places imply a certainty you do not have.

questions.workedExample:
A fair benchmark changes only one thing: the code under test.

- Same machine, same data, same conditions (rules out D).
- Realistic data sizes (B).
- Warm-up, then many repetitions (A, C).
- Report a range or a robust statistic, not one number (rules out E).

The `timeit` docs suggest using the minimum of repeated runs for snippets, since slower runs are usually caused by interference rather than the code itself.

questions.prompt: A service's memory grows by about 50 MB an hour until the container is OOM-killed after roughly a day. Which approach is most likely to find the cause quickly?

options.text: Use `tracemalloc` (or a heap profiler) to take snapshots an hour apart and compare them to see which lines allocated the growing memory
options.explanation: Correct. Comparing snapshots isolates allocations that keep growing. Typical findings: an unbounded dict used as a cache, a list of every request processed, or listeners never removed.

options.text: Increase the container's memory limit to 8 GB
options.explanation: That only delays the crash. A steady leak will eventually exhaust any limit.

options.text: Run cProfile to see which functions use the most CPU
options.explanation: CPU time and memory retention are different questions. A leak can come from a cheap function called often.

options.text: Call `gc.collect()` after every request
options.explanation: Garbage collection frees unreachable objects. Leaked memory is usually still reachable (e.g. from a global cache), so forcing collection will not free it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Steady growth over hours suggests something accumulating, not a one-off spike.
2. Take a snapshot after warm-up, then another an hour later:
   - `snap2.compare_to(snap1, "lineno")` lists lines whose allocations grew the most.
3. Suppose the top line is `_cache[key] = result` in a module with no eviction: that dict grows forever.
4. Fix with a bounded cache (`functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...)` or a TTL cache with a capacity limit and effective expiration) and confirm memory now plateaus. If RSS grows without corresponding traced allocations, investigate native allocations and allocator behavior with suitable tools.

questions.prompt: You need to profile a production Python service that is intermittently slow. Restarting it is undesirable, and you cannot add more than a few percent overhead. Which tool fits best?

options.text: `cProfile`, enabled by restarting the service under `python -m cProfile`
options.explanation: This particular command requires a restart; cProfile can also be enabled programmatically in a running process if instrumentation exists. Its per-call overhead must be assessed.

options.text: Adding `print(time.time())` around every function and redeploying
options.explanation: Requires a deploy, adds I/O to every call, and produces unmanageable output.

options.text: Running the same code on a laptop with `timeit`
options.explanation: A laptop micro-benchmark will not reproduce production data, load or the intermittent condition.

options.text: A sampling profiler such as `py-spy`, attached to the running process by PID
options.explanation: Correct among these choices. External attachment can avoid restart, subject to platform/security permissions. Measure its overhead at the chosen sample rate rather than assuming a fixed percentage.

questions.workedExample:
1. Constraints: no restart, low overhead, real production behaviour.
2. The offered cProfile launch requires restart, while programmatic activation needs integration and incurs per-call cost.
3. Sampling profilers take periodic stack snapshots. py-spy runs as a separate process and can attach by PID.
4. Typical commands:

```
py-spy top --pid 4321
py-spy record -o out.svg --pid 4321
```

(Attaching to another process usually needs root, e.g. `sudo`.)

The SVG is a flame graph of what the service was doing during the slow period. Verify the profiler meets the overhead limit on this workload.

questions.prompt: Your load test reports a p99 latency of 40 ms. Production users report frequent multi-second waits under the same request rate. The load generator uses 10 threads, each sending a request and waiting for the response before sending the next. Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Assume production arrivals continue independently while earlier requests wait.

options.text: When the server stalls, the generator stops sending requests, so the slow period contributes few samples and the percentiles look better than reality
options.explanation: Correct. This is coordinated omission: the tool unintentionally coordinates with the system under test and omits the requests that would have queued up.

options.text: A constant-rate load generator that records latency from each request's intended send time gives a more honest p99
options.explanation: Correct. Tools like wrk2 schedule requests at a fixed rate, so a stall shows up as many slow requests, as it would for real users.

options.text: The mean latency would have been a better metric than p99
options.explanation: The mean hides tail latency even more. The problem is how samples were collected, not which statistic was used.

options.text: The difference must be caused by the production network, since load tests are always accurate
options.explanation: Closed-loop load generators systematically under-report tail latency during stalls; the test itself is a likely cause of the discrepancy.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under the specified production model, requests arrive independently: if the server stalls for 2 s, requests keep arriving and all wait.
2. A closed-loop generator with 10 threads sends at most 10 requests during that stall. Hundreds of 'would-have-been' slow requests are never sent.
3. Result: the stall contributes maybe 10 slow samples out of 100,000, so p99 looks fine.
4. Fix: generate load at a constant rate (open loop) and measure latency from the scheduled send time.

questions.prompt: Profiling a Django view shows 301 database queries for a page listing 300 orders, each displaying its customer's name. What is the problem and the usual fix? Assume customer is a ForeignKey and these are the only queries.

options.text: The database is too slow; add read replicas
options.explanation: Replicas spread load but each of the 301 round trips still costs latency. The query pattern is the problem.

options.text: An N+1 query pattern: one query for the orders plus one per order for its customer; fix it by fetching customers in the same query or one batched query
options.explanation: Correct. In Django, `select_related('customer')` joins the customer in the original query, reducing 301 queries to 1.

options.text: Too many columns are being selected; use `.only()`
options.explanation: Narrower rows help slightly, but 301 round trips remain.

options.text: Python is slow at rendering templates; cache the HTML
options.explanation: Caching hides the cost for repeat visitors but leaves every cache miss doing 301 queries.

questions.workedExample: One orders query plus 300 lazy ForeignKey lookups is N+1. select_related("customer") joins this single-valued relation and reduces this access pattern to one query. With an illustrative fixed 2 ms round-trip overhead, 301 trips contribute 602 ms before database work; a joined query has one trip but its execution cost still needs measurement. Many-to-many relations require prefetch_related rather than select_related; a simple prefetch normally adds one batched query.

lessons.title: Agile, Scrum, Kanban and estimation
lessons.summary: What the Agile Manifesto actually says, how Scrum and Kanban work and differ, Little's law for flow, and how to estimate and forecast honestly with story points, ranges and Monte Carlo simulation.
lessons.body:
The label "Agile" is used for a variety of software processes. In practice that word covers everything from small, self-organising teams shipping daily to heavyweight processes with more meetings than releases. To work well in any of them, it helps to know what the ideas actually are and why they exist.

## The problem Agile was solving

The traditional **waterfall** model runs in phases: gather all requirements, design everything, build it, test it, release. Sequential planning is easier when requirements are stable, but safety-critical or contractual work does not by itself justify deferring integration, feedback or validation.

Software requirements can change or remain uncertain. Users only know what they want once they see something; markets move; technical unknowns surface mid-build. A waterfall project discovers these problems at the end, when changing course is most expensive. (Winston Royce's 1970 paper, often cited as the origin of waterfall, actually described the purely sequential version as risky and recommended iteration.)

## The Agile Manifesto

In 2001, seventeen practitioners met in Snowbird, Utah, and wrote the **Manifesto for Agile Software Development**. It is four lines:

- **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools
- **Working software** over comprehensive documentation
- **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation
- **Responding to change** over following a plan

It adds: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." Agile does not mean no documentation or no plan. It means you deliver working software in short cycles, get feedback, and adjust, because that is cheaper than being wrong for a year.

Scrum and Kanban are two approaches used to organise work and feedback.

## Scrum

Scrum is a framework for working in fixed-length iterations called **Sprints**. The official definition is the *Scrum Guide* by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, last revised in 2020. It is short (under 15 pages) and much of what people call "Scrum" is not in it.

### The Scrum Team

A small team, typically 10 or fewer people, with three accountabilities:

- **Product Owner**: maximises the value of the product; owns and orders the Product Backlog.
- **Scrum Master**: helps the team and organisation use Scrum effectively; causes the removal of impediments to team progress. This accountability is not a project-manager role.
- **Developers**: everyone doing the work of creating a usable Increment each Sprint, including testers and designers.

### Events

| Event | Timebox (1-month Sprint) |
|---|---|
| Sprint | One month or less |
| Sprint Planning | Up to 8 hours |
| Daily Scrum | 15 minutes |
| Sprint Review | Up to 4 hours |
| Sprint Retrospective | Up to 3 hours |

For shorter Sprints, Planning, Review and Retrospective are usually shorter; the Daily Scrum remains a 15-minute event. The Guide does not prescribe a most-common Sprint length.

- **Sprint Planning** answers why this Sprint is valuable (the **Sprint Goal**), what can be done, and how.
- **Daily Scrum** is for the Developers to inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. The 2020 Guide dropped the old "three questions" format.
- **Sprint Review** shows stakeholders what was done and decides what to do next. It is a working session, not a demo for applause.
- **Sprint Retrospective** looks at how the team works and picks improvements.

### Artefacts and commitments

| Artefact | Commitment |
|---|---|
| Product Backlog | Product Goal |
| Sprint Backlog | Sprint Goal |
| Increment | Definition of Done |

The **Definition of Done** is a shared, explicit quality bar (for example tested, reviewed and documented; exact criteria depend on the product and organisation). Work that does not meet it is not part of the Increment, however close it is.

> [!note] Not in the Scrum Guide
> Story points, velocity, user stories, burndown charts and planning poker are all common practices, but none is required by Scrum.

## Kanban

Kanban comes from Toyota's production system, where cards ("kanban" means signboard) signalled when to produce more. David J. Anderson adapted it for software in the mid-2000s.

Kanban does not prescribe roles or iterations. Useful practices include:

1. **Visualise the workflow** on a board, with a column per stage.
2. **Control work in progress (WIP)** with explicit policies; limits may cover individual stages or a larger part of the workflow.
3. **Manage flow**: measure how work moves and remove blockages.
4. **Make policies explicit**, such as what "ready for review" means.
5. **Improve continuously** using data and feedback loops.

```
| To do | Dev (3) | Review (2) | Done |
|-------|---------|------------|------|
| F     | C       | A          | X    |
| G     | D       | B          | Y    |
| H     | E       |            |      |
```

The numbers are WIP limits. With Dev full at 3, a developer who finishes C does not start F; they help clear Review first. This is **pull**, not push: work moves when there is capacity downstream. Stop starting, start finishing.

### Little's law

Why limit WIP? **Little's law** from queueing theory says, for a stable system over the long run:

```
avg WIP = throughput x avg cycle time
```

Rearranged: average cycle time = average WIP / average throughput, using the same workflow boundary and time units.

> [!example] Halving WIP
> In a stable workflow, average throughput is 4 items/week and average WIP is 12, so average cycle time is **3 weeks**. If average WIP becomes 6 while average throughput remains 4, average cycle time becomes **1.5 weeks**. A WIP cap is not the measured average, and this does not promise that every item finishes twice as fast.

Lower WIP may reduce context switching, but excessive restriction can starve stages and reduce throughput. Measure both flow and capacity.

### Scrum versus Kanban

| | Scrum | Kanban |
|---|---|---|
| Cadence | Fixed Sprints | Continuous flow |
| Roles | PO, SM, Developers | None required |
| Planning focus | Sprint Goal and evolving plan | Flow and WIP policies |
| Useful measures | Goal outcomes and product value | WIP, throughput, work-item age, cycle time |

Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably (operations, support, platform teams). Scrum suits product development where a regular rhythm of planning and review helps. Kanban can also complement Scrum. Sprint scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as learning occurs without endangering the Sprint Goal.

## Estimation

Every business needs some answer to "when will it be ready?" Estimation is hard for well-understood reasons.

- **Unknowns.** Much of software work is discovering what needs doing.
- **The cone of uncertainty.** Steve McConnell, building on Barry Boehm's work, illustrates a possible early range of 0.25× to 4× in his cone model. It is not a universal statistical confidence interval. Reducing uncertainty requires decisions and learning; elapsed time alone does not narrow it.
- **The planning fallacy.** Kahneman and Tversky showed people systematically underestimate their own tasks, even when they know similar tasks overran. Hofstadter's law: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's law."

McConnell also separates three things that are often confused. An **estimate** is a prediction ("probably 6–10 weeks"). A **target** is a desired outcome ("launch by the conference"). A **commitment** is a promise. Conflating them turns honest estimates into negotiations.

### Relative estimation: story points

Relative estimation is one technique for discussing size and uncertainty. **Story points** size work relative to a reference item ("this is about twice the login page"), often on a rough Fibonacci-like scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. The growing gaps express growing uncertainty: there is no meaningful difference between 14 and 15.

**Planning poker** uses simultaneous revelation to reduce anchoring on the first spoken estimate: everyone reveals a card at once. If one person says 2 and another 13, they discuss, and usually one of them knows something the other does not. That conversation is the most valuable part.

**Velocity** is points completed per Sprint, used to forecast how much the team can take on. It only works within one team: points are not comparable across teams.

### Ranges and three-point estimates

A single number hides uncertainty. A **three-point estimate** gives optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P) values. The PERT formula weights them:

```
expected = (O + 4M + P) / 6
O=2, M=4, P=12 days
(2 + 16 + 12) / 6 = 5 days
```

Under this PERT weighting model the estimated mean (5) is above the mode (4), reflecting the asymmetric inputs. Three inputs alone do not establish the true distribution, and not every duration distribution is right-skewed.

### Forecasting from data: Monte Carlo

If the team tracks how many items it finishes each week, it can forecast without estimating individual items. Simulate the future by sampling from past throughput:

```python
import random
random.seed(42)

# items finished in each past week
history = [3, 5, 2, 6, 4, 4, 1, 5]

def weeks_to_finish(backlog):
    done, weeks = 0, 0
    while done < backlog:
        done += random.choice(history)
        weeks += 1
    return weeks

runs = sorted(weeks_to_finish(40)
              for _ in range(10_000))
print("50%:", runs[5_000])
print("85%:", runs[8_500])
```

Average throughput is 30 / 8 = 3.75 items a week. The seeded example prints 11 weeks at the 50th percentile and 13 weeks at the 85th. These are model outputs, not guaranteed real-world probabilities. Resampling assumes this short history represents future throughput, weeks can be sampled independently, remaining items are comparable and the backlog stays fixed. Changes in scope, staffing or dependence can invalidate the forecast.

Some teams take this further with **#NoEstimates**: split work into small, similar-sized items and forecast purely from throughput.

## Brooks's law

Fred Brooks, in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975): "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." New people need training from existing members, and the number of possible pairwise communication links grows as n(n−1)/2: a team of 5 has 10, a team of 10 has 45. These are possible links, not a claim that every pair communicates or that actual overhead must be quadratic. Adding people can help on separable work; evaluate onboarding and coordination costs.

## Pitfalls

- **Cargo-cult Scrum.** All the ceremonies, none of the feedback. Ignoring feedback that requires adaptation undermines the Review; it need not change the backlog on every occasion.
- **Velocity as a performance target.** Goodhart's law: once points are a measure of productivity, they inflate. Velocity is a planning tool for the team.
- **Converting points to hours.** It discards the reason for relative sizing.
- **Ignoring the retrospective.** A retro that picks no action, or never checks last time's action, is a wasted hour.
- **Single-number estimates treated as promises.** Give ranges with a confidence level, and re-forecast as you learn.

## Key takeaways
- Agile favours short feedback cycles over big upfront plans; it does not mean no planning or no docs.
- Scrum has three accountabilities, five timeboxed events and three artefacts, each with a commitment (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done).
- Kanban visualises flow and limits WIP; by Little's law, cycle time = WIP / throughput, so reducing average WIP reduces average cycle time if throughput stays fixed and the stable-system assumptions hold.
- Estimates are uncertain by nature: use relative sizing, ranges, three-point estimates or Monte Carlo forecasts from real throughput.
- Keep estimates, targets and commitments distinct, and remember Brooks's law when a project is late.

## Further reading
- [Manifesto for Agile Software Development](https://agilemanifesto.org/)
- [The Scrum Guide (2020)](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html)
- [Kanban (development) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanban_(development))
- [Little's law — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little%27s_law)
- [Planning poker — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_poker)
- [Cone of Uncertainty — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_of_Uncertainty)
- [Brooks's law — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks%27s_law)

questions.prompt: A manager says: "We're Agile now, so we don't write documentation or make plans." What does the Agile Manifesto actually say?

options.text: That documentation and plans should be abolished
options.explanation: The Manifesto explicitly says there is value in the items on the right (documentation, plans); it just values the items on the left more.

options.text: That working software is valued *over* comprehensive documentation, and responding to change *over* following a plan, while the latter still have value
options.explanation: Correct. The Manifesto is about priorities, not prohibitions: plan and document enough to deliver working software and adapt as you learn.

options.text: That plans are required but documentation is optional
options.explanation: The Manifesto treats both the same way: valued, but less than working software and responding to change.

options.text: Nothing about documentation; it only covers team size
options.explanation: Documentation appears directly in the second value. The Manifesto says nothing about team size.

questions.workedExample:
The four values each have the form 'X over Y':

1. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
2. Working software over comprehensive documentation.
3. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
4. Responding to change over following a plan.

Then: 'while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.' So the manager's reading is a common misinterpretation.

questions.prompt: According to the 2020 Scrum Guide, which of these is **not** one of the Scrum events?

options.text: Sprint Retrospective
options.explanation: The Retrospective is one of the five events: the team inspects how it works and plans improvements.

options.text: Daily Scrum
options.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers.

options.text: Backlog Grooming Meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Refining the Product Backlog is an ongoing activity in Scrum, not a formal event. The five events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.

options.text: Sprint Review
options.explanation: The Review is an event where stakeholders inspect the outcome and adapt the backlog.

questions.workedExample:
The Scrum Guide lists five events:

```
Sprint          (container)
Sprint Planning
Daily Scrum     15 min
Sprint Review
Retrospective
```

Product Backlog refinement is described as an ongoing activity, often done in sessions teams schedule themselves, but it is not one of the events.

questions.prompt: A Kanban board has a WIP limit of 3 on the "Review" column, which currently holds 3 cards. A developer finishes coding a card. What should they do under Kanban principles?

options.text: Move the card into Review anyway and note that the limit was exceeded
options.explanation: Ignoring the limit defeats its purpose: it exists to make the bottleneck visible and stop work piling up.

options.text: Start a new card from To Do so they stay busy
options.explanation: Starting more work while downstream is full increases WIP and cycle time. 'Stop starting, start finishing.'

options.text: Help clear the Review column, for example by reviewing one of the waiting cards, then move their card when there is space
options.explanation: Correct. Kanban is a pull system: work moves only when the next stage has capacity. Helping the bottleneck increases flow for everyone.

options.text: Raise the Review WIP limit to 4
options.explanation: Limits can be tuned over time with data, but raising them whenever they bite removes their value.

questions.workedExample:
1. The WIP limit says Review is at capacity.
2. Pushing more work in would create a queue; starting new work elsewhere adds to WIP.
3. The bottleneck is review capacity, so the most useful action is to add capacity there: review someone's card.
4. Once Review has a free slot, the finished card is pulled in.
5. If Review is constantly full, that is a signal to change the process, e.g. smaller PRs or pairing.

questions.prompt: A team finishes on average 5 items per week and in a stable workflow has an average of 20 items in progress. Using Little's law, what is the average cycle time, and what happens if average WIP is cut to 10 with throughput unchanged?

options.text: 4 weeks, falling to 2 weeks
options.explanation: Correct. Cycle time = WIP / throughput = 20 / 5 = 4 weeks. With WIP 10: 10 / 5 = 2 weeks.

options.text: 0.25 weeks, rising to 0.5 weeks
options.explanation: This divides throughput by WIP. Little's law is WIP = throughput × cycle time, so cycle time = WIP / throughput.

options.text: 100 weeks, falling to 50 weeks
options.explanation: This multiplies WIP by throughput. That product has no meaning here.

options.text: 4 weeks, unchanged, since throughput did not change
options.explanation: With throughput fixed, cycle time is proportional to WIP. Halving WIP halves cycle time.

questions.workedExample:
Little's law: L = λW.

```
L = avg WIP         = 20 items
λ = throughput      = 5 items/week
W = avg cycle time  = L / λ
                    = 20 / 5 = 4 weeks
```

With L = 10: W = 10 / 5 = 2 weeks. This is an average, not a promise for each item. A lower WIP cap alone does not establish the new average; throughput can also change.

questions.prompt: In planning poker, three developers estimate a story as 3 points and one estimates 13. What should happen?

options.text: Take the average, about 5.5, and round to 5
options.explanation: Averaging hides the disagreement, which usually means someone knows about risk or complexity the others do not.

options.text: Go with 3, because the majority voted for it
options.explanation: Majority voting ignores the information the outlier has. If they are right, the story is badly underestimated.

options.text: Ask the high and low estimators to explain their reasoning, then re-vote
options.explanation: Correct. The value of planning poker is the conversation the spread triggers. Perhaps the '13' knows the payment API has no sandbox, or the '3's know a library already does it.

options.text: Take the highest estimate to be safe
options.explanation: Padding everything to the most pessimistic estimate skips the discussion and inflates the whole plan.

questions.workedExample:
1. Everyone reveals at once, reducing anchoring on the first number spoken.
2. A big spread signals different assumptions about the work.
3. Low and high estimators explain: 'I assumed we reuse the existing form' vs 'the legacy API needs a new auth flow'.
4. The team now shares the same picture and re-votes. Often the result converges, and sometimes the story is split.
5. The estimate improves, but the shared understanding is the bigger win.

questions.prompt: A task has a three-point estimate of optimistic 3 days, most likely 5 days and pessimistic 13 days. What is the PERT expected duration?

options.text: 5 days
options.explanation: That is the most likely value alone. PERT weights it by 4 but also includes the optimistic and pessimistic values.

options.text: 6 days
7 days
options.explanation: This is the simple average (3 + 5 + 13) / 3, which gives the most likely value no extra weight.

options.text: 8 days
options.explanation: Check the arithmetic: the weighted sum is 36, and 36 / 6 = 6.

questions.workedExample:
PERT expected value = (O + 4M + P) / 6.

```
O = 3, M = 5, P = 13
(3 + 4*5 + 13) / 6
= (3 + 20 + 13) / 6
= 36 / 6
= 6 days
```

The result is above the most likely value because the pessimistic tail (13) is much further from M than the optimistic one (3). This is the PERT model estimate for these inputs; nonnegative duration alone does not prove that a distribution is right-skewed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are signs of a team using Scrum's form without its substance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sprint Reviews ignore stakeholder feedback even when it reveals needed Product Backlog changes
options.explanation: Correct. The Review should enable inspection and adaptation; ignoring actionable feedback defeats that purpose.

options.text: Management compares velocity across teams to rank their productivity
options.explanation: Correct. Story points are team-relative; comparing them across teams is meaningless and encourages point inflation (Goodhart's law).

options.text: Retrospective actions are chosen but never carried out or checked anywhere
options.explanation: Correct. Choosing improvements without implementation or follow-up does not deliver adaptation.

options.text: The Developers adjust their plan during the Daily Scrum when they discover a blocker
options.explanation: That is exactly what the Daily Scrum is for: inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt.

options.text: The team keeps a clear, shared Definition of Done
options.explanation: A Definition of Done is a commitment in the Scrum Guide. Having one is healthy, not cargo cult.

questions.workedExample:
Scrum is built on empiricism: transparency, inspection and adaptation. For each option ask, does the team actually adapt?

- A: inspection without adaptation.
- B: velocity turned into a target, so it stops being a useful measure.
- C: adaptation chosen but never carried out.
- D and E are healthy practices described by the Guide.

questions.prompt: A team has finished between 2 and 7 items a week over the last 12 weeks. 60 similar-sized items remain. A stakeholder asks for "the date". Which answer is most useful and honest?

options.text: A single date based on the average throughput, presented as a commitment
options.explanation: A mean-based date is not automatically a median or a promise. Its miss probability is unknown without a distribution.

options.text: A Monte Carlo forecast using the actual weekly history, with conditional completion percentiles, explicit assumptions and regular updates
options.explanation: Correct. Use the complete samples and explain representativeness, scope and dependence assumptions. A 2–7 range alone cannot determine percentiles; recalculation can widen as well as narrow uncertainty.

options.text: Refuse to estimate, since software cannot be predicted
options.explanation: Businesses need forecasts to plan. Data-based forecasts are cheap to produce and are generally more reliable than gut feel.

options.text: Ask each developer to estimate every remaining item in hours and add them up
options.explanation: Bottom-up hours take a long time, suffer from the planning fallacy on every item, and ignore interruptions and unplanned work that historical throughput already includes.

questions.workedExample: Collect all 12 actual weekly throughput values; the minimum and maximum alone are insufficient. If the history is representative, resample weeks until 60 comparable items finish, repeat and report simulated quantiles. State assumptions about independent weeks, fixed scope and stable capacity. No numerical finish percentiles are supplied here because the complete history is absent and they cannot be reliably calculated. Update the forecast when assumptions or evidence change.

questions.prompt: A 5-person team is three months behind on a project. The director proposes adding 5 more engineers immediately. Which effect does Brooks's law highlight?

options.text: Doubling the team will halve the remaining time
options.explanation: That assumes work is perfectly divisible and new people are instantly productive. Brooks's point is that neither is true for a late project.

options.text: New engineers increase velocity immediately because they are fresh
options.explanation: New engineers need context: the codebase, the domain, the tooling. That takes time and attention from existing members.

options.text: Brooks's law only applies to teams larger than 50
options.explanation: There is no such team-size threshold. Potential pairwise links grow quadratically, but actual communication depends on team structure.

options.text: Potential pairwise communication links grow from 10 to 45 and existing members must spend time onboarding newcomers, so the project is likely to slow down further in the short term
options.explanation: Correct. With n people there are n(n−1)/2 pairs: 5×4/2 = 10 and 10×9/2 = 45. Onboarding also pulls the most knowledgeable people away from the work.

questions.workedExample:
1. Possible pairwise links, not necessarily active communication paths: n(n − 1) / 2.

```
n = 5:   5*4/2  = 10
n = 10:  10*9/2 = 45
```

2. Onboarding: each new person needs explanation, review and pairing from existing members, whose output drops.
3. Partitioning: some tasks cannot be split. Brooks's example: bearing a child takes nine months, however many people are assigned.
4. Alternatives: cut scope, move the date, or add people only to cleanly separable work with clear interfaces.

questions.prompt: A product manager says: "Engineering estimated 8 weeks, sales promised the client 6 weeks, so engineering has committed to 6." Which statements reflect good estimation practice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Eight weeks is an engineering estimate; sales made a six-week promise, but that is not automatically an agreed engineering commitment
options.explanation: Correct. Separate the forecast, desired date and who made or accepted a promise, then reconcile them explicitly.

options.text: The right response is to explore options to meet the target, such as reducing scope or phasing delivery
options.explanation: Correct. When a target and an estimate disagree, the useful conversation is about scope, resources or date, not about making the estimate smaller.

options.text: Engineering should re-estimate at 6 weeks, since estimates should match business needs
options.explanation: Changing an estimate to match a target does not change the work. It only hides the risk until the deadline is missed.

options.text: Estimates early in a project carry wide uncertainty, so the 8 weeks should come with a range
options.explanation: Correct. The cone of uncertainty means early estimates can be off by a large factor; a range with a confidence level is more honest.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the three ideas: estimate (8 weeks, ideally a range), target (6 weeks), sales commitment (already promised, but not yet agreed by engineering).
2. When they conflict, negotiate the *plan*, not the estimate: what can ship in 6 weeks? Can part ship later?
3. Re-estimating to fit (C) is the planning fallacy made official.
4. Give the estimate as a range: e.g. '7–11 weeks, 8 most likely', narrowing as work proceeds.

questions.prompt: A platform team handles a constant, unpredictable stream of requests from other teams, many of them urgent. Two-week Sprints keep being disrupted. Which approach is likely to fit better?

options.text: Longer, four-week Sprints so more work fits
options.explanation: Longer Sprints make the disruption worse: urgent requests would wait even longer or break the Sprint more often.

options.text: Waterfall, with all requests gathered up front for the quarter
options.explanation: Requests are unpredictable by nature; they cannot be gathered up front.

options.text: Remove all process and work on whatever is loudest
options.explanation: Without visualisation or limits the team loses track of work, and the loudest requester always wins.

options.text: Kanban: visualise work, control WIP and track flow without requiring a Sprint cadence
options.explanation: Correct. Kanban's continuous flow handles work that arrives unpredictably. Urgent items can be pulled as capacity frees up, and WIP limits stop the team drowning.

questions.workedExample: A continuous-flow approach may fit interrupt-driven work. Scrum also permits scope adaptation while preserving its Sprint Goal; the fit depends on whether that goal remains useful. Define workflow and urgent-work policies, control WIP and measure cycle times by request type. Derive service forecasts from those observations rather than promising an invented three-day percentile.

lessons.title: Working in teams - docs, review, on-call and postmortems
lessons.summary: The practices that let a team of engineers work as more than the sum of its parts - Conway's law and bus factor, design docs and the four kinds of documentation, effective code review, a sustainable on-call rotation, and blameless postmortems.
lessons.body:
Past a certain size, the hardest problems in software are not technical. A brilliant engineer who leaves no documentation, blocks every review and burns out on call creates less value than a merely good engineer who makes the whole team faster.

This lesson covers the habits that scale knowledge and keep a team healthy: how team shape affects system shape, writing things down, reviewing code, carrying a pager sustainably, and learning from failure. (The System Design module covers SLOs, error budgets and service-level incident response; here the focus is the team.)

## Teams shape systems

**Conway's law** (Melvin Conway, 1968): organisations that design systems "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations". Eric Raymond's tongue-in-cheek restatement: "If you have four groups working on a compiler, you'll get a 4-pass compiler."

It works in both directions:

- If two teams must coordinate on every change to a shared module, consider whether module boundaries or team responsibilities create avoidable coordination. Some coordination may be inherent in the domain.
- The **inverse Conway manoeuvre** deliberately shapes teams to match the architecture you want. Align team ownership with business capabilities and appropriate service boundaries; a team can own several services, and organisation alone does not guarantee independence.

The **bus factor** (or truck factor) is the number of people who would have to disappear before a project stalls. A bus factor of one is a single point of failure: holidays, illness or a resignation stop work, and that person cannot take a real break. Raise it deliberately with pairing, rotating ownership, documentation and review.

## Writing things down

Spoken knowledge does not scale and does not survive staff changes. Good teams write.

### Design docs

Before building anything substantial, write a short **design doc** and have it reviewed. The goal is to find the expensive mistakes while they are still cheap to fix: on paper, not in production. A common structure, used widely at Google and elsewhere:

1. **Context and scope**: what problem, for whom, and why now.
2. **Goals and non-goals**: non-goals are as important; they stop scope creep and endless debate.
3. **The design**: APIs, data model, key flows, a diagram.
4. **Alternatives considered**: and why they lost. This is often the most valuable section for future readers.
5. **Cross-cutting concerns**: security, privacy, observability, migration, cost.

Keep it as short as the problem allows. A two-page doc that people actually read beats a 30-page doc that they skim. Once decided, record significant choices as Architecture Decision Records (covered in the architecture module) so the *why* outlives the meeting.

### The four kinds of documentation

The **Diátaxis** framework points out that documentation serves four different needs, and mixing them makes each worse:

| Kind | Reader wants to |
|---|---|
| Tutorial | Learn by doing |
| How-to guide | Achieve a specific task |
| Reference | Look up facts |
| Explanation | Understand why |

A README that is half tutorial, half API reference and half architecture essay serves nobody. Separate them, and keep docs next to the code (**docs as code**) so they are reviewed and updated in the same pull request as the behaviour they describe.

**Runbooks** are a special case of how-to guide: step-by-step instructions for operational tasks and alerts. Every alert that can page someone should link to a runbook that says what it means, how to check impact and what to try first.

## Code review

Code review catches defects, but its bigger benefits are spreading knowledge (raising the bus factor) and keeping the codebase consistent.

Google's published engineering practices give a useful standard: reviewers should favour approving a change once it **definitely improves the overall health of the code**, even if it is not perfect. Perfectionism in review slows everyone and drives people to batch work into huge, unreviewable changes.

Practical habits:

- **Small changes.** Smaller coherent changes are easier to understand and review; line counts alone do not determine review quality. Split refactoring from behaviour change (see the refactoring lesson).
- **Fast responses.** Google's guide says one business day is the maximum time to respond to a review request. Slow reviews are a hidden tax on every engineer.
- **Comment on the code, not the person.** "This loop is O(n²); a set would make it O(n)" rather than "why would you do this?".
- **Label severity.** Prefix optional suggestions with `Nit:` so the author knows what blocks approval.
- **Automate the trivial.** Formatters and linters in CI settle style, so humans spend review time on design and correctness.
- **Explain the why** in the PR description: context, approach, how it was tested, and what the reviewer should focus on.

## On-call that people can sustain

If your team runs production services, someone needs to respond when they break at 3 a.m. Done badly, on-call burns people out and drives them away. Done well, it is a manageable part of the job that also teaches people how the system really behaves.

### Rotation design

Google's SRE book gives concrete guidelines worth knowing:

- No more than about **25%** of an engineer's time should be spent on call.
- With a primary and a secondary on call around the clock and week-long shifts, the ideal coverage calculation gives **eight engineers** for a single-site team, before leave and other resilience needs. Google separately recommends about **six per site** for dual-site teams, considering both coverage and critical team mass.
- Google reports around **6 hours** of work per incident in its experience, including diagnosis and follow-up, and uses at most **2 incidents per 12-hour shift** as a workload guideline. This is not a universal incident-duration estimate.
- Response expectations cited by Google: about **5 minutes** for user-facing, time-critical services, about **30 minutes** for less time-sensitive ones.

A **follow-the-sun** rotation across suitable time zones and shift lengths can avoid night duty, with clear handovers. Check that the roster covers all 24 hours: London and San Francisco each working an ordinary eight-hour day do not provide complete coverage.

Other essentials:

- **A secondary** and a clear escalation path, so nobody is alone with a problem beyond them.
- **Handover notes** at the end of each shift: what fired, what is still open, what to watch.
- **Compensation and recovery**: pay or time off for on-call, and a lie-in after a bad night.
- **Training**: shadow shifts and practice incidents before someone carries the pager alone.

### Alert hygiene

The SRE book's test for a page: it should detect something **urgent, actionable and actively or imminently user-visible**. Every page should require human judgement; if a script could handle it, automate it.

Common failures and fixes:

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Pages on CPU > 80% without service risk | Tie pages to actionable current or imminent service risk |
| Same alert fires daily | Fix the cause; downgrade or remove only if paging is unnecessary |
| Alert with no runbook | Add a runbook; keep necessary service-risk detection |
| 20 alerts for 1 outage | Group and deduplicate |

**Alert fatigue** is dangerous: when most pages are noise, people stop treating them as urgent, and the real one gets missed. Review every page from the last rotation in a weekly meeting and ask "was this worth waking someone for?".

## Postmortems: learning, not blame

After a significant incident, the team writes a **postmortem**: what happened, the impact, the timeline, contributing factors and follow-up actions. The service-level mechanics (severity levels, incident command, SLO triggers) are in the System Design reliability module. What matters at team level is the culture around it.

A postmortem is **blameless**. It assumes everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and asks why the system made the mistake easy. "Alice ran the wrong migration" leads nowhere; "the migration tool runs against production by default with no confirmation" leads to a fix.

Blamelessness is not about being nice. It is practical: if people are punished for honest mistakes, they hide them, and the organisation stops learning. Amy Edmondson's research on **psychological safety** (a shared belief that it is safe to admit mistakes and take interpersonal risks) found an association with team learning (not a guarantee of causation in every team), and Google's internal Project Aristotle study of team effectiveness reported it as the most important factor of the five it identified.

What makes a postmortem worth writing:

- **Action items with owners and dates**, tracked like any other work. Untracked actions can create false confidence and leave preventable risks unaddressed.
- **Contributing factors, not a single root cause.** Real incidents usually involve several: a bug, a missing alert, a confusing dashboard.
- **Sharing.** Other teams learn from your failures cheaply. Many companies hold a regular postmortem review.

## Team health in general

- **Onboarding** is a test of your docs. Have every new joiner fix whatever confused them.
- **Pairing and mobbing** spread knowledge fast, especially on unfamiliar code.
- **Async by default** for things that do not need a meeting: written proposals, recorded decisions, threads rather than calls. Protect focus time.
- **Rotate ownership** of components and of on-call so expertise is not concentrated.

## Pitfalls

- **Hero culture.** Celebrating the person who fixes everything at 2 a.m. rewards the bus factor of one that caused the problem.
- **Docs written once and never updated.** Wrong documentation is worse than none. Keep docs near the code and change them in the same PR.
- **Review as gatekeeping.** Blocking on style preferences, or leaving reviews for days, teaches people to avoid review.
- **Paging on causes rather than symptoms.** High CPU alone need not page, but imminent exhaustion that threatens users and requires urgent human action can justify a page.
- **Blameless in name only.** If a postmortem's real outcome is someone being quietly sidelined, the next incident will be reported later and less honestly.

## Key takeaways
- Conway's law links team structure to system structure; design both together, and raise the bus factor deliberately.
- Write short design docs with goals, non-goals and alternatives; separate tutorials, how-tos, reference and explanation; keep docs next to code.
- Review small changes quickly, approve changes that improve code health, and automate style.
- Google’s illustrative on-call model needs at least eight people for two single-site roles at 25% duty and targets at most two incidents per 12-hour shift; adapt staffing and workload to the service, including leave, runbooks and recovery.
- Blameless postmortems with owned, tracked actions turn incidents into learning; psychological safety is what makes them honest.

## Further reading
- [Being On-Call — Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/being-on-call/)
- [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure — Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)
- [Google Engineering Practices: Code Review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/)
- [Design Docs at Google — Malte Ubl](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/)
- [Diátaxis documentation framework](https://diataxis.fr/)
- [Conway's law — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway%27s_law)
- [Psychological safety — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_safety)

questions.prompt: Only one engineer understands the billing reconciliation job. She is about to take three weeks of leave. What concept describes the risk, and what is the best longer-term response?

options.text: Technical debt; rewrite the job before she leaves
options.explanation: A rushed rewrite before she leaves adds risk and still leaves the knowledge in one head (hers, about the old version).

options.text: A bus factor of one; spread knowledge through pairing, a runbook and rotating ownership
options.explanation: Correct. The bus factor counts how many people would have to vanish before work stalls. Raising it means getting the knowledge into other heads and onto paper.

options.text: Conway's law; reorganise the team
options.explanation: Conway's law relates org structure to system structure. The problem here is concentrated knowledge, not team shape.

options.text: Alert fatigue; reduce the job's alerts
options.explanation: Alert volume is unrelated to how many people understand the job.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count the people who could keep the job running without help: one. Bus factor = 1.
2. Short term: a handover session and a written runbook before the leave.
3. Longer term:
   - Pair on the next changes to the job.
   - Put a second person on its on-call rotation.
   - Document how it works and how to recover it.
4. The goal is that her leave, or her leaving, is a non-event.

questions.prompt: A README contains a getting-started walkthrough, a full list of configuration options, an essay on why the system uses event sourcing, and steps to rotate the database password. According to the Diátaxis framework, what is wrong?

options.text: Nothing; all documentation should be in one file
options.explanation: One file is not the issue. Mixing four kinds of documentation in one flow means each reader has to wade through material meant for someone else.

options.text: Configuration options should never be documented
options.explanation: Reference documentation for configuration is essential; it just belongs in a reference section.

options.text: Design rationale belongs only in code comments
options.explanation: Explanations of architecture are too broad for comments. They belong in explanation docs or ADRs.

options.text: It mixes a tutorial, reference material, an explanation and a how-to guide, which serve different needs and are better separated
options.explanation: Correct. A learner, someone looking up an option, someone wanting to understand a design choice and someone doing a task each need a differently shaped document.

questions.workedExample:
Map each part to a Diátaxis kind:

```
getting-started    tutorial
config options     reference
event sourcing     explanation
rotate password    how-to guide
```

Each has a different reader. Split them into separate pages (perhaps linked from a short README), so a tired on-call engineer looking for the password steps does not have to scroll past an essay.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a postmortem to be **blameless**?

options.text: No one is allowed to mention who performed which action
options.explanation: Postmortems name actions and actors in the timeline. Blameless means not punishing them for reasonable actions, not hiding facts.

options.text: The incident is attributed to bad luck so nobody feels responsible
options.explanation: Blamelessness still looks for causes; it seeks them in systems and processes, not in luck.

options.text: It assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew, and looks for the conditions in the system that made the mistake possible or likely
options.explanation: Correct. The question becomes 'why did the system make this easy to do?', which leads to fixes like safer defaults, better tooling or clearer alerts.

options.text: Only managers write it, to protect the engineers involved
options.explanation: The people closest to the incident usually write it, because they know what happened.

questions.workedExample:
1. Contrast two findings:
   - 'Bob deleted the wrong table.' Outcome: Bob is careful for a while.
   - 'The admin tool connects to production by default and has no confirmation for destructive commands.' Outcome: a fix that protects everyone.
2. Blamelessness gets you the second kind, because people are honest when they are not punished for reasonable mistakes.
3. It does not remove accountability: the team is accountable for completing the action items.

link.title: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure — Google SRE book

questions.prompt: A team wants a 24/7 on-call rotation with a primary and a secondary at all times, week-long shifts, and no engineer on call more than 25% of the time. They are all in one office.
